detail_ebpf_subtitle: Measuring CPU, memory, and I/O latency inside the Linux kernel
detail_ebpf_overview: The delays that decide end-to-end performance are usually invisible from user space. A process waits in the run queue, stalls on a page fault, or blocks on a device, and from the outside all three look the same: the program is slow while the CPU looks fine. Answering which of the three it is needs timestamps taken inside the kernel, on both sides of the event. This toolkit takes those timestamps for scheduling, memory, and block I/O, and reports each as a latency distribution rather than an average.
detail_ebpf_point1: Three eBPF tools — runqlat, memlat, iolat — that time run-queue wait, page-fault handling, and block I/O inside the kernel and export log2 latency histograms.
detail_ebpf_point2: A shared command-line interface (--duration, --out) and a one-click collection script, so every tool is run the same way and two runs can be compared.
detail_ebpf_point3: CSV histograms with a matching .summary.json per run, stored next to the environment metadata for that run.
detail_ebpf_arch_body: Each tool is an eBPF program attached to a pair of kernel tracepoints plus a small user-space control program. The kernel side stores an entry timestamp in a BPF hash map, computes the delta at the exit tracepoint, and increments a log2 bucket in a histogram map. Nothing is sent to user space per event. The Go collector reads the histogram map once the measurement window closes and serialises it. Nothing in the observed application is modified or recompiled.
detail_ebpf_fig_pipeline: One measurement path: a tracepoint pair gives the delta, the delta is bucketed in a BPF map inside the kernel, and the Go collector reads the map once per run and writes one CSV and one JSON summary per tool.
detail_ebpf_pipeline_step1: Attach eBPF programs to the entry and exit tracepoints for scheduler wakeup, page fault, and block I/O.
detail_ebpf_pipeline_step2: Store the entry timestamp in a BPF hash map keyed by the event, compute the delta on exit, and add it to a log2 bucket. Per-event data never crosses into user space.
detail_ebpf_pipeline_step3: After a fixed duration the Go collector reads the histogram maps and serialises them, together with the metadata of the machine the run happened on.
detail_ebpf_pipeline_step4: scripts/collect_all.sh --duration 30s --out results/... runs all three tools in sequence and writes memlat.csv, runqlat.csv, and iolat.csv with matching .summary.json files.
detail_ebpf_validation_item1: Scheduling latency shows a long tail under load even when CPU utilisation looks normal, which is exactly the case an average hides.
detail_ebpf_validation_item2: Memory access latency stays flat until page faults are induced; then the tail buckets spike while the median barely moves.
detail_ebpf_validation_item3: Block I/O latency clusters by request size and device behaviour, so the slow requests are identifiable rather than merely present.
detail_ebpf_takeaway: The output of every run is a distribution, and the interesting part of all three distributions is the tail. Fixed durations and one output format are what make two tails comparable at all.
detail_ebpf_debug_symptom: Measurements of the same workload disagreed between runs, and there was no way to tell whether a difference was real or an artefact of how the run was started.
detail_ebpf_debug_hypothesis: Each tool had its own duration handling, its own output shape, and no record of the machine state, so runs from different sessions were not comparable in the first place.
detail_ebpf_debug_tests: Standardised duration and output format across the three tools, then reran identical workloads repeatedly to see how much the histograms varied between runs.
detail_ebpf_debug_fix: One CLI, one fixed-duration collection path, and environment metadata written next to every result set.
detail_ebpf_debug_takeaway: The measurement method has to be as fixed as the workload. Ad-hoc tracing produces numbers; a fixed method produces numbers you can compare.
detail_ebpf_design_item1: Compute deltas in the kernel and export only histograms. Sending one record per event to user space would cost more than the latency being measured.
detail_ebpf_design_item2: Bucket by log2 rather than report an average. The tail is the part users feel, and a mean over a long-tailed distribution reports neither the common case nor the bad one.
detail_ebpf_design_item3: Give all three tools the same flags and the same output format. Comparing a CPU histogram with an I/O histogram is the whole point, and that only works if they are shaped alike.
detail_rowscope_title: RowScope: DRAM Row Buffer Locality Analyzer
detail_rowscope_subtitle: Quantifying how memory access patterns drive DRAM row buffer hit rates
detail_rowscope_overview: DRAM performance is shaped by how an access pattern lands on banks and rows, not only by how much bandwidth a program asks for. An access to the row already open in a bank is cheap; an access to a different row in the same bank forces a precharge and an activate first. Profilers report cache misses and bandwidth, but not that distinction, and the hardware counters that would report it need elevated privilege and differ between CPU generations. RowScope answers one question for a known access pattern: what fraction of its accesses find the row already open?
detail_rowscope_point1: A five-stage pipeline — C benchmarks, address traces, DRAM address mapper, per-bank row buffer state machine, results aggregator — that labels every access as a row hit, a row miss, or a row conflict.
detail_rowscope_point2: A closed-form model, hit rate = 1 − stride × 4 / 8192, checked against the simulated result at 11 stride values from 1 to 1024 elements.
detail_rowscope_point3: A 250x locality gap between sequential access (99.95% hit rate) and random access on a 16 MB array (0.4%), and nine log-spaced working sets from 512 KB to 128 MB showing that sequential locality does not depend on array size.
detail_rowscope_arch_body: RowScope never touches a real memory controller. A C benchmark writes the virtual addresses it touches into a trace file with a metadata header. A Python mapper decomposes each address into a bank, a row, and a column offset under a configurable geometry — 8 KB rows and 8 banks by default — using a bit-interleaved scheme. The trace is then replayed through one row buffer state machine per bank, which is what turns an address sequence into hit, miss, and conflict counts.
detail_rowscope_fig_address: Address decomposition. With an 8 KB row and 4-byte elements, the low 13 bits of an address are the column offset, the next bits select the bank, and the rest is the row id — which is why a stride below 2048 elements keeps landing in the same open row.
detail_rowscope_fig_state: Row buffer state per bank. From EMPTY the first access is a miss; while row r is OPEN an access to r is a hit and an access to any other row is a conflict, paying a precharge and an activate before it can be served.
detail_rowscope_pipeline_step1: Four C benchmarks (sequential_access.c, random_access.c, stride_access.c, working_set_sweep.c) execute a controlled access pattern and write the virtual addresses they touch, with a metadata header, to a .trace file.
detail_rowscope_pipeline_step2: dram_mapping.py decomposes each address into (bank_id, row_id, col_offset) for a configurable row size and bank count, defaulting to 8 KB and 8 banks.
detail_rowscope_pipeline_step3: row_buffer_model.py keeps an OPEN or EMPTY state per bank and classifies each access as a row hit, a row miss, or a row conflict in constant time.
detail_rowscope_pipeline_step4: Per-benchmark hit, miss, and conflict rates plus a locality score are written to summary.csv, and six figures are generated from it with Matplotlib.
detail_rowscope_pipeline_step5: report/final_report.md is filled from a template with those tables and figures, so the whole experiment reruns from one shell script.
detail_rowscope_stat2_label: Row hit rate, random access on 16 MB
detail_rowscope_evidence1: rowscope-plot.png — simulated row hit rate (left axis) and row conflict rate (right axis) against stride, for strides of 1 to 1024 elements with an 8 KB row and 4-byte elements. Hit rate stays above 87% up to stride 256 and collapses beyond it.
detail_rowscope_takeaway: The access pattern decides row buffer locality, and the working set size barely matters: sequential access holds 99.95% from 512 KB to 128 MB, while random access on 16 MB drops to 0.4% with a 99.6% conflict rate. The stride sweep follows 1 − stride × 4 / 8192 closely enough that the row size can be read back off the curve.
detail_rowscope_design_item1: Simulate in user space instead of reading hardware counters. Counters such as UNC_M_CAS_COUNT need elevated privilege and change between CPU generations, and simulation makes the DRAM geometry a parameter rather than a property of the test machine.
detail_rowscope_design_item2: Treat malloc virtual addresses as if they were physical. Page allocation for large arrays is not deterministic, but every workload is analysed under the same mapping, so the systematic error cancels in a comparison between patterns — it would not cancel in an absolute prediction.
detail_rowscope_design_item3: Model the open-page policy only. It is the common DDR4 policy and the only one that produces the three-way hit, miss, and conflict split this project is about; closed-page and adaptive policies are left out rather than approximated.
detail_can_title: CAN Bus Security Analysis and Intrusion Detection
detail_can_subtitle: Bit-level multi-signal packing and rate-based anomaly detection on a simulated ECU network
detail_can_overview: CAN has been the standard bus between vehicle ECUs since 1986, and it carries no sender authentication. Any node with bus access can transmit any identifier, and every node receives every frame, which is the structural reason spoofing, sniffing, and message injection all work. Our six-person team analysed the data frame field by field and rebuilt a working transmitter, receiver, monitor, and intrusion detector in LabVIEW. Instead of conventional ECU signals we packed six human biometric signals into the payload, which made the bit-packing design something we had to derive rather than copy.
detail_can_point1: A 64-bit signal map for six signals — LFT 10, HEM 19, BRAIN 21, WATER 3, GENDER 1, STRESS 10 bits — that fills the data field exactly, with no overlap and no unused bits.
detail_can_point2: Symmetric transmit and receive bit packing in LabVIEW Formula Nodes using AND, OR, and shift, verified byte by byte against hand-computed patterns.
detail_can_point3: A rate-based intrusion detector: the receive loop measures the actual packet interval, switches the hazard LED to red when it exceeds the configured rate, and stops the loop in the same cycle.
detail_can_arch_body: The demonstrator is a single LabVIEW VI with two loops. The transmit loop takes six signal values, packs them into byte0 through byte7 in a Formula Node, and joins them into a uint8[8] array that stands for the data field of a frame with identifier 5 and DLC 8. The receive loop indexes that array, runs the inverse bit operations, drives the monitoring gauges, and feeds the rate monitor that decides whether traffic looks injected.
detail_can_fig_frame: The standard CAN data frame: SOF 1 bit, arbitration 12 (11-bit identifier and RTR), control 6, data 0 to 64, CRC 16, ACK 2, EOF 7. Only the data field carries payload, and no field identifies the sender.
detail_can_fig_packing: The 64-bit payload map. Bit boundaries were computed by hand and chain exactly: 0+10, 10+19, 29+21, 50+3, 53+1, 54+10 = 64. Signals cross byte boundaries, so byte1 holds LFT bits 9 to 8 together with HEM bits 5 to 0.
detail_can_fig_ids: Packet arrival intervals against the configured rate. While the measured interval matches the threshold the indicator stays green; once it exceeds the threshold the indicator turns red and the receive loop stops on the same iteration.
detail_can_pipeline_step1: The transmit Formula Node masks and shifts the six values into eight bytes, for example byte1 = ((LFT & 0x300) >> 8) | ((HEM & 0x3F) << 2).
detail_can_pipeline_step2: Build Array joins byte0 through byte7 into the uint8[8] payload, transmitted with identifier 5 and DLC 8.
detail_can_pipeline_step3: The receive Formula Node applies the inverse operations, for example LFT = ((byte1 & 0x03) << 8) | byte0, and writes the six values to the front panel indicators.
detail_can_pipeline_step4: A comparison tab shows the transmitted and reconstructed byte arrays side by side, which is how a wrong bit boundary becomes visible immediately.
detail_can_pipeline_step5: The receive loop measures the packet interval, compares it against the configured rate, raises the hazard LED and terminates the loop when the interval exceeds it.
detail_can_takeaway: With all six signals at maximum (LFT 1023, HEM 524287, BRAIN 2097151, WATER 7, GENDER 1, STRESS 1023) every transmitted byte reads 0xFF and the receiver reconstructs the original values; a mid-range BRAIN of 100000 reproduces the expected pattern across byte3 to byte6. Stepping the receive interval 200 → 210 → 250 → 300 ms against a 200 ms threshold trips the alert and stops the loop within one cycle.
detail_can_design_item1: Pack six signals into one frame rather than sending one frame per signal. The data field is fixed at 8 bytes, so six separate frames would carry the same information at six times the bus load.
detail_can_design_item2: Detect intrusion by packet rate rather than by payload content. CAN offers no sender authentication, so timing is the only signal available without changing the protocol — and the cost is real: a forged frame sent at the normal rate is invisible to this detector.
detail_can_design_item3: Carry fractional and negative values with a x100 scale and a +100 offset instead of widening the fields. Two's complement would consume the whole 10-bit STRESS field, while a shared offset costs no bits at all; the price is that everything below the second decimal is lost.
detail_5g_oran_subtitle: Bringing up Open5GS, srsRAN, and the O-RAN SC RIC as one working chain
detail_5g_oran_overview: A 5G stack is four independent programs that only work in one order: core, RIC, base station, handset. Reading about the interfaces between them does not tell you what each one prints when it is ready, or which failure belongs to which layer. The goal of this lab was to bring the whole chain up on a shared server with no radio hardware, and to write down the exact command and the exact confirmation signal for every step.
detail_5g_oran_point1: Brought up the four components in order — Open5GS 5GC under Docker Compose, the O-RAN SC RIC, an srsRAN gNB with E2 enabled, and srsUE in its own network namespace.
detail_5g_oran_point2: Ran the entire chain over ZMQ radio emulation on a remote lab server reached by SSH, using the upstream gnb_zmq.yaml and ue_zmq.conf configurations rather than hand-written ones.
detail_5g_oran_point3: Documented a gNB start-up failure end to end: the error, the four things I checked, and the fact that none of them was the cause.
detail_5g_oran_arch_body: srsUE talks to an srsRAN gNB over a ZMQ radio link, so no SDR hardware is involved. The gNB connects north to the Open5GS core — the AMF address it dials has to match the NGAP address inside the core container's amf.yaml — and sideways to the O-RAN SC RIC over E2. The core and the RIC each run as their own Docker Compose stack, and the UE runs in a separate Linux network namespace so its traffic stays separable from the host's.
detail_5g_oran_fig_bringup: Bring-up order with the signal that each step is up: the 5GC with a reachable AMF, the RIC printing "RMR is ready now...", the gNB started with -c gnb_zmq.yaml e2, and finally srsUE inside namespace ue1.
detail_5g_oran_pipeline_step1: docker compose up 5gc in srsRAN_Project/docker starts Open5GS; docker exec into the open5gs_5gc container confirms the AMF NGAP address the gNB will need.
detail_5g_oran_pipeline_step2: docker compose up in oran-sc-ric brings up the RIC. The log line "RMR is ready now..." is the point at which it will accept an E2 connection.
detail_5g_oran_pipeline_step3: ./gnb -c gnb_zmq.yaml e2 with the AMF address and local bind address set, using the configuration file downloaded from the srsRAN documentation.
detail_5g_oran_pipeline_step4: ip netns add ue1 creates the namespace, then ./srsue ue_zmq.conf starts the handset; a successful attach completes the chain from core to UE.
detail_5g_oran_validation_item1: The 5GC container reports its services running before the gNB is started, and amf.yaml inside the container shows the NGAP address the gNB configuration has to match.
detail_5g_oran_validation_item2: The RIC prints "RMR is ready now...", which is the readiness signal for the E2 termination.
detail_5g_oran_validation_item3: After the rebuild the gNB and the UE both start, and core, RIC, gNB, and UE run together as one chain.
detail_5g_oran_takeaway: The stack comes up in exactly one order, and each step has one line of output that says whether to continue. Recording those four lines is what turned a session of guesswork into a lab someone else can repeat.
detail_5g_oran_debug_symptom: The gNB exited during start-up with an INI error reporting that it could not read a section of cu_cp.amf, so no E2 session was ever established.
detail_5g_oran_debug_hypothesis: The AMF address in the YAML was wrong; or the gnb_e2ap.pcap file that E2AP logging writes to was missing; or its filename in the YAML did not match the file on disk; or its path or permissions blocked the write.
detail_5g_oran_debug_tests: Read amf.yaml inside the open5gs_5gc container and confirmed the NGAP address matched the configuration. Confirmed gnb_e2ap.pcap existed, compared the filename in the YAML against the file, relaxed the file permissions, and moved the file to another directory with the path updated. The same error appeared every time.
detail_5g_oran_debug_fix: None of the four was the cause. The checked-out srsRAN source was out of date; rebuilding from the current upstream instructions made the same configuration work.
detail_5g_oran_debug_takeaway: The error named a configuration section, so I spent the session inside the configuration. A correct configuration can still fail because of the environment around it, and the version of the program producing the message is now the first thing I check, not the last.
detail_5g_oran_design_item1: Run every component in its own container or namespace instead of on the host. The core, the RIC, and the UE all want their own network stack, and the namespace is what keeps the UE's traffic separable.
detail_5g_oran_design_item2: Use ZMQ radio emulation instead of an SDR front end. There is no radio hardware in the lab, and ZMQ makes the whole chain reproducible over an SSH session on a shared server.
detail_5g_oran_design_item3: Take configuration files from the upstream documentation rather than writing my own. When the gNB failed that made my configuration the least likely explanation, which is exactly how the search ended up on the source version.
detail_opencl_title: On-Device GPU Image Processing via OpenCL and the Android NDK
detail_opencl_subtitle: An 8.4x Gaussian blur speedup from JNI-bridged OpenCL kernels on a mobile GPU
detail_opencl_overview: A Gaussian blur computes a weighted average over each pixel's neighbourhood. On a CPU that is a serial pass over every pixel; on a GPU it is one work-item per pixel and the arithmetic is unchanged. This project tested that difference on an actual Android board, which meant writing the OpenCL host code by hand against the NDK: at the time almost nothing was documented about running OpenCL on Android, so the driver was built up call by call from the Khronos guide.
detail_opencl_point1: Wrote OpenCLDriver.c from scratch — platform and device enumeration, context and command queue, runtime kernel build, buffer I/O, NDRange dispatch, and explicit release of every OpenCL object.
detail_opencl_point2: Exposed four native methods to the Java activity through JNI (GaussianBlurBitmap on the CPU, GaussianBlurGPU, GaussianGreyGPU, GaussianRotateGPU), all sharing one driver path that differs only in the .cl file and the kernel name.
detail_opencl_point3: Timed each path from Java with System.nanoTime(): the same blur takes 2059 ms on the CPU and 246 ms on the GPU, an 8.4x speedup with no change to the algorithm.
detail_opencl_arch_body: The Java activity holds an ARGB_8888 bitmap and calls a native method. The driver locks the bitmap with AndroidBitmap_lockPixels, copies the pixels into a staging buffer so the original survives, initialises OpenCL, reads and builds the .cl file at run time, writes the pixels into a device buffer, dispatches a one-dimensional NDRange over all pixels with a local work size of 64, reads the result back, releases every OpenCL object, unlocks the bitmap, and hands it back to Java for display.
detail_opencl_fig_stack: One call path: Activity (Java) → JNI → OpenCLDriver.c → clBuildProgram and clEnqueueNDRangeKernel → Mali GPU. Pixels cross the same boundary twice, between AndroidBitmap_lockPixels and clEnqueueWriteBuffer on the way in and clEnqueueReadBuffer on the way out.
detail_opencl_pipeline_step1: CMake 3.22 compiles OpenCLDriver.c into a shared library and links libGLES_mali.so together with jnigraphics and the Android log library.
detail_opencl_pipeline_step2: The driver reads the bitmap's width, height, stride, and format, checks it is RGBA, and copies the pixels into a native staging buffer.
detail_opencl_pipeline_step3: clGetPlatformIDs, then clGetDeviceIDs with CL_DEVICE_TYPE_GPU, clCreateContext, and clCreateCommandQueue, with every call wrapped in an error-check macro that logs the OpenCL error code.
detail_opencl_pipeline_step4: The .cl file for the requested operation is read from the device, built with clCreateProgramWithSource and clBuildProgram, given the source buffer, destination buffer, width, and height as arguments, and enqueued as a 1-D NDRange over all pixels with a local size of 64.
detail_opencl_pipeline_step5: clEnqueueReadBuffer copies the result into the locked bitmap, every OpenCL object is released, the bitmap is unlocked, and the processed image returns to the ImageView.
detail_opencl_evidence1: opencl-result.png — output of the three GPU kernels on the test image, photographed from the device for the project slides: original, Gaussian blur, grayscale, and rotation.
detail_opencl_takeaway: Measured on the device with System.nanoTime(): Gaussian blur 2059 ms on the CPU against 246 ms on the GPU, grayscale 81 ms, rotation 72 ms. Blur costs more than the other two on the GPU because each work-item reads a neighbourhood instead of a single pixel; grayscale and rotation touch one pixel each and finish under 100 ms.
detail_opencl_debug_symptom: On the target board the application crashed on launch whenever the camera preview was part of the build, even though the permission was declared in AndroidManifest.xml.
detail_opencl_debug_hypothesis: The same crash had appeared in an earlier lab when the camera permission was handled incorrectly, so that was the first hypothesis; the second was an incompatibility between the board's Android version and the Camera API it was being called with.
detail_opencl_debug_tests: Corrected and re-checked the permission both in the manifest and at run time, and the crash stayed. Rebuilt the same preview and capture flow in a separate project on the same board, where it ran without a problem, which removed the permission hypothesis without identifying a replacement.
detail_opencl_debug_fix: The root cause was never found. I removed the camera preview, capture, and hold path and loaded a stored image with BitmapFactory.decodeFile instead, which left the OpenCL pipeline — the actual subject of the project — intact and measurable.
detail_opencl_debug_takeaway: Isolating the camera proved where the fault was not, never where it was. Cutting an unexplained subsystem out to protect the deliverable was the right call against the deadline; closing the project without an explanation is the part I would not repeat.
detail_opencl_design_item1: Copy the pixels into a staging buffer instead of processing the bitmap in place. The original image has to survive so the user can return to it and run a different filter on the same input.
detail_opencl_design_item2: Keep one driver path for all three GPU kernels and vary only the .cl file and the kernel name. The OpenCL host code is identical for all of them, so three copies would have meant fixing the same bug three times.
detail_opencl_design_item3: Compile the kernel at run time from a file on the device rather than embedding it in the library. A kernel can then be edited and rerun without rebuilding and reinstalling the APK.
detail_dynamic_moh_title: GPU Memory System Optimization for LLM Inference
detail_dynamic_moh_subtitle: MoH-guided head-wise offloading: routing traces, head regularity, and the transfer cost of acting on them
detail_dynamic_moh_overview: LLM inference is bounded by attention-related memory cost: the KV cache footprint, the traffic it generates, and the host-device transfers that follow when it does not fit. Mixture-of-Head attention already produces a per-token signal about which heads matter. If that signal is stable enough, it can drive a memory decision — keep these heads resident, move those to host memory — instead of only a compute decision. This project tests whether that holds, and what it costs when it does.
detail_dynamic_moh_question: Can MoH routing signals reduce effective attention cost, by using fewer heads or treating heads differently, without hurting output quality?
detail_dynamic_moh_arch_body: The target is a Mixture-of-Head attention model served with PyTorch and Transformers, with hooks on the router output that log which heads each token selects. Attention state lives in GPU memory; host DRAM is far larger but sits behind PCIe. Any head-wise offloading plan therefore has two costs that do not appear in a head count: the transfer of head state across PCIe, and the stalls when that transfer is not overlapped with compute. The router trace tells us which heads a policy would keep; the transfer measurement tells us whether keeping them is worth anything.
detail_dynamic_moh_fig_arch: Where the cost sits. Attention state is resident in GPU memory, host DRAM is large but a PCIe crossing away, and every head-wise offloading decision pays for that crossing whether or not it saves compute.
detail_dynamic_moh_fig_trace: Token by head selection grid recorded from the router. If neighbouring tokens select the same heads, a residency policy can reuse them; the Jaccard similarity between adjacent columns is how that regularity is measured rather than assumed.
detail_dynamic_moh_fig_overlap: The same two layers on two timelines. Serial: the transfer for layer i+1 starts after layer i finishes computing. Prefetch: the transfer runs underneath the compute, and only the uncovered part still costs time.
detail_dynamic_moh_pipeline_step1: Run inference on controlled prompts with scripts/run_router_trace.py and log per-token head selection and router scores to a trace file.
detail_dynamic_moh_pipeline_step2: Plot head activation frequency and Jaccard similarity between neighbouring tokens and across layers, to test whether selection is regular enough for a residency policy to predict.
detail_dynamic_moh_pipeline_step3: Vary the fraction of heads kept and measure output quality against it, then extend the same sweep to latency, throughput, peak GPU memory, PCIe bytes, and overlap ratio.
detail_dynamic_moh_pipeline_step4: Evaluate naive offloading, keep-hot with a window tau, and prefetch with overlap, recording for each what it has to know in advance and where it loses.
detail_dynamic_moh_finding1_body: There is a gentle regime where dropping heads costs little quality, and a threshold past which the loss becomes sharp. The useful question is where that knee sits, not whether it exists.
detail_dynamic_moh_finding2_body: Head selection is less regular than the offloading idea needs. Similarity between neighbouring tokens is not high enough to justify a simple reuse heuristic, so a policy built on "the same heads stay hot" would misfire more often than the trace plots first suggested.
detail_dynamic_moh_finding3_body: Fewer active heads does not mean less time. Whether a head-wise policy wins depends on transfer size, pinned memory, and overlap, so the system metrics have to be measured alongside quality rather than after it.
detail_dynamic_moh_debug_symptom: Reducing the number of heads, or introducing offloading, sometimes produced almost no gain and sometimes made the run slower than the baseline.
detail_dynamic_moh_debug_hypothesis: Many small transfers dominate the latency; or pageable memory and synchronous copies prevent any overlap with compute; or the router tracing itself is heavy enough to contaminate the timings.
detail_dynamic_moh_debug_tests: Microbenchmarked host-to-device and device-to-host bandwidth against transfer size, and copy-compute overlap separately; then ran ablations that toggled logging, batched the transfers, and separated trace collection from the timed run.
detail_dynamic_moh_debug_fix: Pinned memory with asynchronous transfers, a coarser transfer granularity, keep-hot with a window tau, and trace collection moved out of any run whose time is being reported.
detail_dynamic_moh_debug_takeaway: Algorithmic sparsity is not a system result. Transfer granularity, pinning, and overlap decide whether a smaller head count turns into a smaller number of milliseconds.
detail_dynamic_moh_next1: Add system metrics to every sweep — latency, throughput, peak GPU memory, PCIe bytes moved, overlap ratio — so a quality loss can be traded against a measured gain instead of an assumed one.
detail_dynamic_moh_next2: Measure host-to-device and device-to-host bandwidth against transfer size on the target GPU, and set the offloading granularity from that curve rather than from the head layout.
detail_dynamic_moh_next3: Run keep-hot and prefetch against a no-offload baseline on identical prompts, and report the prompts where the policies lose as well as the ones where they win.
detail_pim_accel_subtitle: Removing atomic contention from the rendering backward pass with bank-local reduction
detail_pim_accel_overview: In a 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM pipeline the time goes into tracking and mapping, and inside those the rendering backward pass dominates. That pass is not short of arithmetic — it is short of independent writes. Many fragments contribute gradients to the same gaussian, so the accumulation becomes a pile of atomic adds onto the same address, and the hardware serialises them. The reformulation here is to stop treating it as a compute problem: bin fragments by memory bank on the host and reduce them inside the bank, so there are no global atomics left to contend for.
detail_pim_accel_question: Can bank-local reduction inside PIM remove the atomic contention that dominates 3DGS-SLAM's rendering backward pass?
detail_pim_accel_arch_body: The workload takes P fragments, each carrying a gaussian_id and a gradient vector of length D, and produces an accumulator array acc[G][D]. On the GPU each fragment does an atomicAdd into acc[gaussian_id]; when many fragments share a gaussian those adds serialise, and the cost grows with the skew of the distribution rather than with the number of fragments. The PIM path bins fragments by bank on the host (gaussian_id modulo the bank count), accumulates locally inside each bank, and writes back only what is needed.
detail_pim_accel_fig_contention: The same fragments on two paths. On the GPU many updates converge on one accumulator element through atomicAdd and serialise there; binned by bank, the same updates are spread across banks and each bank sums its own share in parallel.
detail_pim_accel_fig_stages: The four stages that all have to be counted: bin on the host, transfer, accumulate in PIM, write back. A comparison that times only the accumulate stage is not a fair comparison.
detail_pim_accel_pipeline_step1: Extract the rendering backward pass into a standalone gradient-accumulation benchmark driven by synthetic or trace-derived fragments, so contention can be varied on purpose.
detail_pim_accel_pipeline_step2: Two baselines, not one: a global atomicAdd version and a block-level reduction version that already removes most of the atomics. The second is what the PIM path actually has to beat.
detail_pim_accel_pipeline_step3: Bank-local reduction in the SAIT PIMSimulator with host-side binning, keeping the split of responsibilities explicit: the host bins, PIM generates addresses and accumulates.
detail_pim_accel_pipeline_step4: Vary P, G, D, and the skew of the fragment-to-gaussian distribution, and report speedup, scaling, and a per-stage breakdown rather than a single number.
detail_pim_accel_finding1_body: GPU and PIM accumulators are compared element-wise under a fixed seed, with maximum absolute error and relative error reported, before any timing number is taken seriously.
detail_pim_accel_finding2_body: GPU kernel latency and atomic pressure on one side; PIM cycles plus host-side data movement on the other, with binning, transfer, accumulation, and write-back timed separately.
detail_pim_accel_finding3_body: The claim to prove is a crossover: as the distribution becomes more skewed, GPU atomics should degrade sharply while bank-local reduction stays flat or degrades slowly. The sweep that would show it has not been run yet.
detail_pim_accel_debug_symptom: Early PIM runs produced either incorrect accumulators or speedups too large to be explained by the compute and memory behaviour of the workload.
detail_pim_accel_debug_hypothesis: The host was doing work that belonged to PIM; or the payload encoding between host and simulator did not match; or the binning layout broke the bank-locality assumption the whole design rests on.
detail_pim_accel_debug_tests: Locked the inputs and compared GPU-Atomic, GPU-BlockReduce, and PIM-Reduce on the identical fragment set, timing the binning, accumulation, and write-back stages separately instead of end to end.
detail_pim_accel_debug_fix: Defined the responsibilities strictly — host bins, PIM generates addresses and accumulates — made the binning layout explicit, and reported per-stage latency in every result.
detail_pim_accel_debug_takeaway: A PIM speedup is only meaningful with the staging cost attached. A number that hides the host's share of the work is not a comparison, it is an accounting choice.
detail_pim_accel_next1: Run the contention sweep over P, G, D, and distribution skew, and produce the speedup-versus-skew curve the whole argument rests on.
detail_pim_accel_next2: Drive the benchmark from real 3DGS-SLAM traces instead of synthetic fragments, so the skew matches what rendering actually produces.
detail_pim_accel_next3: Report host binning as part of the PIM total, and find the skew below which paying for binning is not worth it.
